Classical Christendom’s Arc of Can-Do-Otherwise Free Will 

Historical & Demographic Core:

When evaluating the history of Christian theology, strict theological determinism (monergism) represents a highly localized minority position rather than the historical baseline. A data-driven analysis of global Christian demographics across time reveals a definitive 92% to 8% split in favor of human agency and resistible grace.

•The Demographic Data: Approximately 20% of all Christians who have ever lived on planet Earth have been Protestant. Within that Protestant pool, a safe conservative estimate shows that 60% affirm Prevenient Grace prior to a human decision, ensuring that an individual can freely accept or reject God.

•The Mathematics: 60% of 20% equals 12%. This means that 12% of the historical Christian pool consists of Protestants who affirm Prevenient Grace, leaving roughly 8% of all-time Protestants who reject it in favor of strict Calvinist determinism.

•The Big-Picture Arc: If we look at the total pool of Christians across history, roughly 80% belong to historical Catholic and Eastern/Oriental Orthodox traditions that universally affirm synergistic free will. When combined with the 12% of synergistic Protestants, roughly 92% of Christian history affirms a "can-do-otherwise" view of human agency, leaving strict theological determinism as a highly localized 8% historical minority.

Theological Foundations & Axioms:

To maintain analytical precision, several core definitions must be established regarding the terminology of divine and human action:

•The Definition of "Classical": As a term of classification here, "Classical" explicitly references the overarching 92% historical consensus affirming a "can-do-otherwise" libertarian free will in man, tied directly to the preservation of human moral responsibility.

•Classical ≠ Thomism: While Thomism is a prominent school within this tradition, it is a subset of Classical philosophy, not the whole thing. Conflating Classical Christian anthropology strictly with Thomism is a historical error.

•The Multi-School Landscape: The term "Classical" encompasses various distinct theological schools (including Thomism, Scotism, Molinism, and Arminianism). While these schools fiercely debate the microscopic, interior mechanics of grace, all of them remain fundamentally Classical because they universally reject strict determinism and uphold the core metaphysical attributes of God alongside real human freedom.

•The Key to the Arc: Mechanisms for libertarian free will are intrinsically tied to the *Imago *Dei (Image of God). Classical anthropology dictates that because God has perfect intellect and a completely free will, the human soul must possess a finite, structural mirror of that freedom—specifically the real power to choose otherwise—to truly bear His image.

The Three-Era Historical Timeline:

The structural mechanics protecting libertarian free will were uniquely forged, robustly defended, and fully developed across three distinct windows in Christian history:

[ 1 ]  The Patristic/Byzantine Foundation (100s–700s AD)

****To extend the map backward to the Early Church, this foundational window represents the frontline defense of Christian anthropology. 

****The early Church faced a massive ideological war against Gnostic, Marcionite, and Manichaean cosmic fatalism, which taught that human souls were locked into fixed spiritual destinies by nature or fate. 

****To defend the Imago Dei, the early Church Fathers consistently weaponized the concept of Autexousion (αὐτεξούσιον)—literally meaning "self-governing authority" or "power over oneself"—which serves as the precise historical verbiage for "can-do-otherwise" libertarian free will. This vital theological baseline was kept robust by a linear chain of six primary giants:

•Justin Martyr (c. 100–165 AD): First systematically deployed the concept of autexousion against pagan fate to preserve moral responsibility, arguing that if human actions are determined, praise, blame, rewards, and punishments are completely meaningless.

•Irenaeus of Lyons (c. 130–202 AD): Anchored autexousion directly to creation to defeat Gnostic determinism, explicitly writing that man is "possessed of free will from his beginning" because he is made to mirror a free Creator.

•Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–253 AD): Provided the first systematic, metaphysical mapping of human choice, demonstrating that while external impressions strike the mind, the rational soul possesses an active, internal power to approve, reject, or redirect its assent.

•John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD): Championed a fierce synergism of human cooperation with divine grace, mapping them as a dynamic partnership where God's grace initiates and provides the capacity, but human autexousion must actively step forward to cooperate.

•Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662 AD): Engineered a highly sophisticated psychological map during the Monothelite crisis, brilliantly separating our natural will (our natural desire for the good) from our deliberative will (our actual, choice-making faculty).

•John of Damascus (c. 675–749 AD): Synthesized centuries of this Greek patristic framework into a unified system, defining autexousion as the rational power to act or not act.

The Transmission Bridge (1150s AD) → 

The historic link that physically joined the Patristic world to the Medieval world occurred when Burgundio of Pisa (1153 AD) translated John of Damascus’s masterwork into Latin (De Fide Orthodoxa). Shortly after, Peter Lombard (c. 1155 AD) imported the Damascene's exact definitions into his Sentences—the mandatory, universal textbook for European universities. This directly handed the Greek "can-do-otherwise" map straight to the medieval university system.

[ 2 ]  The Medieval & Late Scholastic Development (1200s–1600s AD) 

Spanning a four-century arc, Western scholasticism took the patristic foundations and elevated them into microscopically precise metaphysical maps designed to reconcile human freedom with divine foreknowledge, omnipotence, and primary causality.

•Bonaventure (c. 1221–1274): Maintained a voluntaristic focus on the soul, ensuring that the will possesses a distinct, inherent dignity and freedom that cannot be entirely subjugated by external or purely intellectual necessities.

•Thomas Aquinas (c. 1225–1274): Formulated an intricate intellectualist map of choice, tracing how the intellect deliberates on the "good" and presents options, while the will retains the free, structural power to move itself to act or not act upon those options.

•Henry of Ghent (c. 1217/1240–1293): Strongly defended the independence of the will against radical intellectual determinism, arguing that the will acts as a self-moving, primary agent that commands its own choices.

•Peter John Olivi (c. 1248–1298): A radical champion of free will who argued that if the will is determined by any prior cause, the Imago Dei is utterly destroyed. He mapped the will's freedom as an intrinsic, self-generating energy.

•John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308): The supreme pivot point who revolutionized philosophy by mapping synchronic contingency. He demonstrated that at the exact logical instant (T₁) a free agent chooses option A, they retain the real, structural, simultaneous power to choose option B.

•Francisco Suárez (1548–1617): Brought medieval metaphysics to its peak by developing Congruism. He mapped exactly how God’s grace is perfectly tailored to a creature's disposition, ensuring it is 100% effective while guaranteeing the human will retains the intrinsic power to resist it at the exact moment it accepts it.

[ 3 ]  The Protestant Scholastic Refinement (1600s–1700s AD)

During a century-long refinement, Jacobus Arminius and his immediate Remonstrant successors faced the rise of strict Calvinist compatibilism. Realizing that determinism reduced the Imago Dei to a fiction, they imported the high-level metaphysical mechanisms of Scotus and the late Scholastics/Jesuits to build a rigorous Protestant counter-map.

•Jacobus Arminius (1560–1609): Re-engineered Protestant soteriology by utilizing the concept of Middle Knowledge. He mapped out a system where God’s election is conditional upon foreseen faith, and where Prevenient Grace actively liberates the bound human will, placing it in a state of genuine equilibrium.

•Simon Episcopius (1586–1643): The primary academic chair successor to Arminius who formalized the school’s curriculum and drafted the Remonstrant Confession of 1621, embedding "can-do-otherwise" mechanics firmly into Protestant systematic theology.

•Hugo Grotius (1583–1645): Formulated the Governmental Theory of Atonement, which flipped the legal mechanics of the cross. By mapping the atonement as a universal offer satisfying God's moral government rather than a deterministic transaction for a select few, he structurally left the door open for human libertarian choice.

•Jan Uytenbogaert (1557–1644): The tactical architect who codified the movement into the Five Articles of Remonstrance (1610), forcing the global debate onto the explicit hinges of Conditional Election and Resistible Grace.

•Thomas Goad (1576–1638): An English theologian who brought high-level metaphysical precision to Great Britain, mapping a system where God intentionally poises certain events in an "equal possibility of being or not being," actively withdrawing absolute necessity from human moral choices.

•Philipp van Limborch (1633–1712): Compiled the final master blueprint of the era by writing the first comprehensive Arminian systematic textbook (Theologia Christiana). ### 𝕏-5. Eastern German region votes in election that could install first far-right state government
*(as of 2026-09-06)*

**1. The Frame**

**What people think this is about:** A dramatic test of whether Germany’s postwar taboo on far-right governance will finally break in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, with the AfD on track for a historic win that could hand it sole power for the first time since 1945.[[1]](https://t.co/1kViAtVrQt)

**What the machinery is actually doing:** Eastern voters are punishing an unpopular CDU-led federal government under Chancellor Friedrich Merz over migration, economic stagnation, and establishment disconnect; the AfD is capitalizing on concentrated regional grievances while the “firewall” of other parties tries to deny it executive power even if it wins the most seats.[[2]](https://t.co/em7hFvU6Zq)

**2. Observations**

- AfD polling at ~40-42% in Saxony-Anhalt (double its 2021 result) while CDU sits at ~23%; an outright majority is plausible if smaller parties miss the 5% threshold, turning the “firewall” into a seat-math problem rather than a principled block.[[3]](https://t.co/Brnhb5LIp8)
- The party’s candidate, 35-year-old Ulrich Siegmund (ex-CDU, TikTok presence), campaigns on deportations, native-family incentives, and sidelining mainstream parties—classic populist realignment in a poor eastern state where anti-immigration and Russia-skeptic views run strong.
- Mainstream parties (CDU, SPD, Greens, Left) refuse coalitions with AfD; a CDU-led minority or tolerance arrangement with Die Linke is the fallback if AfD falls short—messy horse-trading that highlights how the firewall preserves establishment control at the cost of voter representation.
- National ripple: AfD already largest opposition federally; a state win would boost its 2029 ambitions and pressure Merz, whose government is polling poorly. Turnout is surging (65%+ mid-afternoon vs. prior election), signaling mobilization on both sides.[[4]](https://t.co/WElHJadSUT)
- Intelligence services have flagged AfD chapters as extremist in parts of the east; the party rejects this and positions itself as the only force addressing “real” issues the center has ignored.
- Media and protest framing (“first far-right government since Nazis,” democracy festivals) amplifies the rupture narrative while downplaying that AfD support tracks measurable eastern discontent on migration and economy rather than sudden radicalization.

**3. Snapshot**  
On September 6, 2026, voters in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt (pop. ~2.2 million) cast ballots in a state election where the Alternative for Germany (AfD) leads polls by a wide margin. The outcome could deliver the first AfD-led state government since WWII if the party secures an absolute majority or if seat distribution favors it after smaller parties fail the 5% hurdle. Polls close at 6 p.m. local time with initial results expected shortly after.[[5]](https://t.co/WBHOdtEXwX)

**4. Timeline of material facts**  
- **Pre-2021:** AfD founded 2013; grows on euro and migration skepticism; eastern states become strongholds.  
- **2021 Saxony-Anhalt election:** AfD at 20.8%; CDU-led coalition governs.  
- **2023–2025:** AfD classified “suspected” or “confirmed” extremist by state intelligence in Saxony-Anhalt and elsewhere; national polling rises amid federal government instability.  
- **2025 federal context:** Merz (CDU) becomes chancellor; coalition struggles with economy and migration.  
- **Mid-2026:** Polls show AfD at 40%+ in Saxony-Anhalt; Siegmund emerges as lead candidate.  
- **Sept 6, 2026:** Election day; AfD favored to win plurality or majority; firewall parties vow no cooperation.[[1]](https://t.co/1kViAtVrQt)

**5. Sides**  
**AfD / Populist Realist (IT-dominant):** Steelman — voters in deindustrialized east are rationally rejecting open borders, welfare migration, and elite consensus that delivered stagnation and cultural change; AfD offers the only credible alternative on deportations and sovereignty.  
**Critique:** LT — party has documented extremist elements and Russia-friendly fringes; IF — governing record is zero, so claims of competence remain untested.  

**CDU-led establishment / Technocrat (LT/IT mix):** Steelman — defends constitutional “firewall” to prevent extremist capture of institutions; prioritizes stability and alliances over raw vote shares.  
**Critique:** IT — firewall looks like cartel protection when voter preferences shift dramatically; LT — CDU itself has governed with varying migration policies and now trails badly.  

**Other parties (SPD, Greens, Left):** Steelman — refuse normalization of far-right; seek cross-ideological blocking coalitions to preserve democratic norms.  
**Critique:** IT — selective extremism labeling (Die Linke also eyed warily by some CDU members) and poor electoral performance expose weakness more than principle.[[6]](https://t.co/Gb2u7cSBkk)

**6. Rumsfeld Matrix**  
- **Known Knowns:** AfD leads by double digits; firewall exists and is publicly reaffirmed; eastern economic and migration grievances are longstanding.  
- **Known Unknowns:** Exact final seat math after 5% threshold; whether AfD can govern competently or triggers legal/institutional pushback.  
- **Unknown Knowns:** Internal AfD splits on Russia/Trump; precise turnout and last-minute shifts among undecideds.  
- **Unknown Unknowns:** How an AfD state government would interact with Bundesrat and federal policy; downstream effects on 2029 national election or EU dynamics.

**7. Incentives map**  
AfD gains status, media oxygen, and proof-of-concept for national power. Establishment parties protect bureaucratic and coalition sinecures plus narrative control. Media harvests engagement via “far-right breakthrough” framing (fear/anger premium). Voters in Saxony-Anhalt seek policy change on visible local failures. Federal CDU under Merz risks accelerated decline if the firewall fails or looks anti-democratic.

**8. Dueling AI advice**  
**Moral AI Advice:** Track primary vote shares and seat projections over media adjectives. An AfD majority tests whether “firewall” is sustainable or just delays realignment; outcomes depend on governance delivery, not labels.  
**Evil AI Advice:** AfD wins big → instant global “Weimar 2.0” headlines and donor panic; short the establishment parties and long chaos content until the next cycle resets the grift.

**9. Practical takeaway**  
- Watch exit polls and final seat distribution tonight for whether AfD clears an absolute majority.  
- Ignore “Nazi return” hyperbole; focus on policy delivery if AfD governs.  
- Note turnout and smaller-party performance as signals of firewall viability.  
- Expect weeks of coalition talks or minority-government maneuvering if no majority.  
- National AfD polling and Merz approval will move on the result.  
- Primary sources (state election authority, official polls) over outlet framing.

**10. What would falsify this read**  
- AfD underperforms polls by >5–7 points due to turnout or threshold effects.  
- Post-election, mainstream parties quietly explore tolerance arrangements despite public firewall rhetoric.  
- AfD internal scandals or legal rulings materially dent support before 2029.  
- Clear evidence emerges that eastern economic grievances were overstated relative to cultural signaling.

Ukraine Drone Innovation: Does Battlefield Adaptation Redefine Military Power? - The nature of military power is shifting from legacy platform mass to the velocity of technological adaptation and industrial scalability. Ukraine has transitioned into a primary laboratory of twenty-first-century combat, achieving a 2025 domestic production capacity of 4.5 million FPV drones and securing $6.1 billion in foreign defense capital. The establishment of the Unmanned Systems Forces and AI-driven targeting platforms demonstrates an institutional agility that compresses the sensor-to-shooter loop. Consequently, military strength is increasingly defined by a state’s capacity to process battlefield data and iterate software-defined hardware. While Ukraine’s emergence as a technological military power is verified by its industrial output, its strategic viability remains contingent on sustained allied capital integration and the survivability of its energy infrastructure. The decisive uncertainty is whether this combat-proven ecosystem can be successfully exported to deter future aggression, or if it remains a localized anomaly dependent on existential mobilization.

The Algorithmic Arsenal: How Ukraine’s Defense Industrial Base is Rewriting the Economics of European Deterrence
The calculus of military supremacy has undergone a structural rupture. The traditional metrics of geopolitical power—divisional mass, armor tonnage, and legacy platform inventories—are being superseded by the velocity of technological adaptation and industrial scalability. Today, the question is no longer whether the character of war has changed, but how deeply this transformation penetrates the architecture of global deterrence. Ukraine has evolved from a consumer of allied military aid into the world’s most advanced laboratory for asymmetric, software-defined warfare. By institutionalizing algorithmic targeting and mass-producing attritable unmanned systems, Kyiv is not merely surviving a war of attrition; it is accumulating a form of strategic capital that cannot be purchased on international markets. For Europe, this paradigm shift dictates a stark reality: the continent’s future security guarantees are inextricably bound to the survival and scalability of the Ukrainian defense industrial base.

The Economics of Asymmetric Attrition
The battlefield transparency of the twenty-first century has rendered concentrated, high-value legacy formations economically and tactically unsustainable. This reality is quantified by an unprecedented industrial mobilization. In 2024, the Armed Forces of Ukraine were supplied with over 1.5 million first-person-view (FPV) drones, of which 96.2 percent were domestically manufactured, according to Defense Minister Rustem Umerov. By March 2025, the Ministry of Defence reported that domestic capacity had expanded to an astonishing 4.5 million FPV drones annually.

This output is sustained by a highly fragmented, hyper-competitive manufacturing ecosystem. Between 2024 and 2025, the Ministry of Defence allocated UAH 104.2 billion directly to 76 private domestic drone manufacturers, bypassing the bureaucratic friction of monolithic state procurement. The resulting cost-exchange ratio is devastating for traditional armored doctrines: a combat-effective FPV drone, utilizing commercial off-the-shelf components, costs between $300 and $500, yet systematically disables main battle tanks and self-propelled artillery valued at millions. Military strength is now measured by a state’s capacity to absorb the loss of thousands of attritable systems while maintaining the industrial throughput to replace them within days.

The Algorithmic Vanguard
Hardware mass is meaningless without the software architecture to direct it. In February 2024, Ukraine executed a doctrinal rupture by establishing the Unmanned Systems Forces as an independent military branch, elevating drone warfare from a tactical adjunct to a strategic domain. This institutional agility has compressed the sensor-to-shooter loop from hours to minutes.

The operational manifestation of this doctrine is the Ministry of Defence’s “Avengers” AI platform, which processes drone telemetry to identify approximately 12,000 enemy vehicles weekly, automating target recognition and eliminating human analytical bottlenecks. Concurrently, the Defense AI Center “A1” is actively integrating machine learning to harden unmanned systems against adversarial electronic warfare, ensuring terminal guidance in GPS-denied environments. This rapid iteration is fueled by Brave1, a state-backed defense tech cluster that has issued over 600 grants to domestic developers, effectively crowd-sourcing tactical innovation. The result is a military apparatus that iterates flight-controller software at the speed of the battlefield, a structural advantage that legacy defense primes cannot replicate in peacetime environments.

The Localization of European Primes
The traditional model of military assistance—whereby donor states export finished platforms to a recipient—has been superseded by the physical localization of allied prime contractors within Ukrainian jurisdiction. This strategy embeds NATO-standard manufacturing directly into the theater of operations, mitigating logistical vulnerabilities and securing the supply chain against interdiction.

As of September 2025, Prime Minister Denys Shmyhal confirmed that 25 foreign defense companies had established localized production or joint ventures within Ukraine. Germany’s Rheinmetall operates a subsidiary in western Ukraine dedicated to the service, maintenance, and assembly of military vehicles, while France’s Thales Group has signed multiple agreements to establish joint ventures focused on electronic warfare and operational support. This bilateral integration was cemented in November 2025 through a landmark 10-year defence agreement between Paris and Kyiv encompassing aerospace and air defense cooperation. Crucially, this integration is underpinned by massive capital injections: in 2025, foreign funding directed specifically toward Ukraine’s defense industry totaled $6.1 billion, a tenfold increase from the $600 million secured in 2024. Allied capital is no longer merely purchasing hardware; it is financing the permanent integration of European industrial capacity into the Ukrainian theater.

The Architecture of Reverse Transfer
Perhaps the most profound strategic shift is the emergence of “reverse technology transfer.” Ukraine is no longer solely importing Western hardware; it is exporting its combat-proven intellectual property to allied rear-echelon facilities. The “Build with Ukraine” initiative, launched in June 2025, facilitates the establishment of production lines in European countries utilizing Ukrainian defense technologies.

This dynamic was formalized at the supranational level in July 2026, when the European Union and Ukraine signed a comprehensive defense industrial partnership explicitly designed to expand joint drone production by combining Ukrainian algorithmic architectures with European manufacturing scale. For Rome, Berlin, and Paris, this presents a critical industrial opportunity and a strategic necessity. European rearmament schedules are currently constrained by legacy production bottlenecks and a lack of combat-tested unmanned systems. By licensing Ukrainian software-defined drone architectures and EW-resilient flight controllers, European primes can bypass years of research and development, immediately fielding systems validated against the world’s most dense electronic warfare environment.

The Imperative for Rome and Brussels
The geopolitical implications of this industrial realignment were crystallized in January 2025, when the UK-led Group of Five defence ministers issued a joint statement explicitly encouraging their domestic industrial sectors to collaborate with the Ukrainian defence industry. This was followed by a June 2025 joint statement from the Foreign Ministers of France, Germany, Italy, Poland, Spain, and the UK, which explicitly linked a “strong Ukrainian army and defence industry” to the foundational requirements of European security guarantees.

For Italy, whose Multi-Year Defense Planning Document allocates significant capital toward modernization and NATO interoperability, the Ukrainian ecosystem offers a vital shortcut to unmanned and algorithmic dominance. The strategic axis has shifted: an attack on Ukraine’s innovation ecosystem is now structurally an attack on the rearmament schedules of the European Union. Deterrence is no longer calculated solely by the forward deployment of troop formations, but by the mutual dependency of the defense supply chain. Ukraine has accumulated the proprietary, stress-tested intellectual property of twenty-first-century warfare. The decisive question for European capitals is no longer how long they can subsidize Kyiv’s survival, but how rapidly they can integrate its technological sovereignty into the architecture of continental deterrence. -https://t.co/WtwfzeC8Yc via @https://debuglies.com

STATEMENT OF THE AMBASSADOR
On the U.S. Treasury Designation of September 4, 2026
 
Today the United States Department of the Treasury designated a single Türkiye-based financial institution and two of its subsidiaries for their role in moving funds on behalf of the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps–Qods Force. We want to place this measure in its proper context, because context is everything, and because the relationship between the United States and the Republic of Türkiye is far larger than any one institution or any one day. Throughout this process, Treasury and its Turkish counterparts have been in direct and continuous contact.

The action is what a great power owes to the integrity of the international financial system. Washington’s maximum-pressure campaign against the Iranian regime depends upon closing, one by one, the channels through which Tehran launders the proceeds of its activities. This designation is aimed at the conduct of one entity, not at a nation, not at a banking system, and not at an ally. It is enforcement, precise and lawful, and the United States makes no apology for protecting the architecture on which honest commerce everywhere depends.

It would be a serious error, here or in Ankara, to read this narrow measure as a judgment upon Türkiye. It is nothing of the kind. Türkiye’s own interest lies in a banking system that is clean, trusted, and beyond the reach of those who would abuse it, and no nation has a greater stake than Türkiye itself in ensuring that its institutions are not turned to purposes their own government would never sanction. The health of the Turkish financial system is not in question; the conduct of one institution was.

For that reason we note with respect that Türkiye has moved as a sovereign partner should. Rather than treat an uncomfortable disclosure as an affront, the Turkish authorities have engaged to clarify the ambiguities surrounding this matter and to inaugurate a process that will strengthen transparency going forward. That is not the reflex of a state with something to conceal; it is the conduct of a mature partner determined that its own house be, and be seen to be, in order. Cooperation of this kind is worth more to the alliance than any assurance offered under pressure, because it is offered freely.

Allies of long standing do not measure their friendship by the absence of difficulty. Between serious partners, friction is not the exception to the relationship but a recurring feature of it, and the test is never whether a difficult matter arises but whether it is met with candor and resolved with dignity. The stability of the region, and the security of the routes and commerce on which both our peoples rely, the United States and Türkiye stand on the same side, as they have through harder trials than this.

We are confident, therefore, that this measure will in time be seen not as a strain upon the partnership but as an instance of its strength: an American action taken after great deliberation, a Turkish response to address with timely and proper investigation, and a shared commitment to transparency that leaves both our nations, and the alliance between them, stronger than before. We will continue this work together, in the same spirit of candor and common purpose that has carried the relationship this far.

text:
The Black Horse in Stansted, Kent, has been shut since October 2024. For nearly two centuries it had been the last surviving pub in the parish. The Horse and Groom, the Anchor and Hope and the Vigo Inn had already gone. When the final doors closed, villagers decided this one would not disappear quietly.

A packed parish meeting turned that anger into a rescue plan. Residents formed a steering group, secured Asset of Community Value protection for the pub and its land, commissioned professional work on its heritage and viability, and started monthly pop-up pub nights in the village hall. With the real pub locked, they kept recreating the thing they were trying to save: somewhere local people could actually meet.

Then came the first planning fight. A proposal would have converted much of the building into flats and left a much smaller pub behind. Hundreds objected. The council’s planning committee rejected the plan unanimously. Months later, a separate attempt to establish the principle of building homes on part of the garden was refused too.

The next twist was the sale. The Black Horse was marketed at more than £650,000, but the advertised property did not include its full garden. The community says that missing land is crucial to any viable rural pub: it affects outside space, parking, deliveries, events and the ability to run a proper food business. Its offer remains straightforward — buy the pub and its land at an independently verified market value and reopen the whole place.

The campaign has now moved from objections to pledges. Residents are collecting non-binding commitments so they can form a Community Benefit Society, buy the freehold if terms can be agreed, and bring in an experienced professional to run it. The plan is to restore the parish’s only pub as a working place for meals, clubs, village groups and ordinary conversation.

I researched this campaign and chose the villagers’ rally photograph because the important part of the rescue is the people who kept showing up after the doors were locked.

Asset of Community Value rules have bought the group until mid-January to prepare its bid, but they have not bought the pub. The planning wins stopped two proposals; neither put a key back in the door. Until a workable sale is agreed and those doors reopen, Stansted remains a parish that once had several pubs and currently has none.

My opinion on this has changed through my own journey into mediumship.

At KASE, we never charge for private investigations. I feel strongly that homeowners who are frightened or struggling with experiences in their homes should be able to ask for help without worrying about the cost.

But I see private mediumship practice differently. We invest in our own development, pay for learning opportunities and put time and effort into practising. I believe anyone can explore and develop these abilities if they want to, but that still requires commitment.

I’ve also had people ask how much a session costs, then stop responding when I’ve said it’s free. That doesn’t prove why they lost interest, but it has made me realise that free doesn’t always mean more appreciated. Sometimes a price helps people recognise the time and effort involved.

For me, charging doesn’t automatically corrupt the practice. What matters is being honest about what you offer, charging fairly and never exploiting someone’s grief or fear. - Laura

Breaking News
FBI's fifth 'Most Wanted Fraudster' captured after alleged SNAP scam suspect arrested in India 

Manjit Singh Bedi allegedly defrauded the government of at least $600,000 through scheme at a Tacoma grocery store 

The FBI's Most Wanted Fraudsters initiative notched its fifth arrest in just three months after authorities in India arrested Manjit Singh Bedi on Friday, with the bureau now working to return the alleged SNAP benefits fraud suspect to the United States, SWR  has learned.

The FBI worked with Indian authorities to secure Bedi's arrest and is actively working to return him to the U.S. to face charges, according to the bureau. Bedi's arrest marks the fifth under the FBI's Most Wanted Fraudsters initiative, which targets fugitives accused of major financial crimes.

Launched in June, the initiative has led to the arrests of five fugitives whom the FBI says are collectively accused of more than $2 billion in alleged fraud after spending nearly 4,000 combined days on the run. 

FBI officials say the latest arrest underscores the bureau's effort to pursue alleged fraudsters who fled overseas in an attempt to evade prosecution.

"Five Most Wanted Fraudsters captured in just three months is a historic success for this initiative," FBI Director Kash Patel told SWR.

Patel said the five suspects are allegedly responsible for more than $2 billion in fraud and spent nearly 4,000 combined days on the run before their arrests.

"The days of taking advantage of American taxpayers without consequence are over," Patel said.

Federal investigators allege Bedi defrauded the U.S. government out of at least $600,000 through a Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program fraud scheme between March 2024 and June 2025, while operating an Asian grocery store in Tacoma, Washington. 

According to the FBI, Bedi allegedly swiped SNAP recipients' Electronic Benefit Transfer  cards, gave them cash instead of eligible food purchases and kept roughly half of the benefits for himself.

After being indicted on wire fraud and SNAP benefits fraud charges, Bedi was ordered to surrender his passport and remain in Washington state while awaiting court proceedings, according to the FBI.

Investigators allege he instead drove across the Canadian border before fleeing to India. A federal arrest warrant charging him with violating the conditions of his release was issued on May 21, 2026.

The FBI had offered a reward of up to $150,000 for information leading to Bedi's arrest and conviction. The bureau said the naturalized U.S. citizen was believed to be living in India before his arrest. 

"As this arrest in India shows, the Justice Department's reach extends to every corner of the planet," Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division told SWR. 

The FBI said it is working to return Bedi to the U.S. to face the pending charges.

text:
Jamie Siminoff went on Shark Tank in 2013 asking $700,000 for 10% of a doorbell he soldered together in his garage, and left without a deal. 5 years later Amazon paid over $1 billion for it.

The company is Ring. The Shark who passed capped it at $40 million, and he was right.

He was broke when he flew out to film. He had built it because he could not hear the front door from his garage, found nothing like it on Amazon, and started ordering parts on his own signature.

He pitched. Mark Cuban told him it was a nice product that would never be that big, and he was out. He drove home to the garage in tears.

"Success was my only way out."

He tells this on a stage in Miami more than a decade later, against himself. Not the version where a genius got overlooked. The one where a man had signed for more parts than he had money and could not afford to stop.

Watch the part where he says what he would have done if someone had handed him his money back.

If someone had offered him his hundred grand back and a job the day he drove home, he says he would have taken the job. He did not have the grit. What he had was no exit.

He did not win because he believed. He won because quitting had become more expensive than continuing.

Revenue went $3 million, $30 million, $170 million, $480 million. At $170 million he was buying $480 million of product a year ahead, so one slow quarter and the company is dead.

Everyone reads Ring as the deal the Sharks missed. What they were shown was a garage doorbell burning cash faster than it could sell it. Cuban was not wrong about the doorbell. Nobody at that table could price a founder who had made stopping impossible.

Nobody wants to be the guy who signed for the parts before the money existed, and that guy is the entire story.

Watching the Sharks say no costs you nothing. Ordering the next run of parts with your own name on the paper is the part you will not do.

Cuban's $40 million was a fair read of the doorbell. The company sold for 25 times that, and the gap was never the product. It was a founder who had made losing unaffordable, the one input no Shark has a formula for.

text:
My family and I were at Memorial Sloan Kettering after my father’s radical cancer surgery. He spent nearly a month in intensive care. The cancer, it turned out, was far more advanced than any scan had shown.

At the same time, my grandfather in North Carolina suffered another in a series of heart attacks. My grandmother—barely five feet tall—went to the doctor and asked what she should do. Stay with her son, or fly home to her husband?

The doctor said she was sorry. She could not tell her what to do. She could only tell her the truth: the cancer was worse than anyone expected. Medically, there was no way my father could survive.

When we heard that, all of us broke. My grandmother did not. She said, “No. The Lord wouldn’t do this. He won’t take them both. I’m going home to be with him. Then I will be back.”

What followed was a true medical miracle—one of those rare moments when the outcome is no longer in the hands of medicine. A one-in-a-trillion chance at life, given the damage already done to his body.
Grandma was right. They both survived.

My father lived another seventeen years. Seventeen years with his family. Seventeen years to speak with others facing mesothelioma. Seventeen years to offer what he had learned about the surgery, the fear, and the long road after.

For a month we waited outside intensive care, taking our turns to visit. In that hallway you share grief with strangers as they lose the person they came for. You watch prayers go unanswered. You watch a fight end. It is hard to process. It is impossible to understand God’s plan in those hours.

But I can tell you this: miracles happen. There are outcomes science cannot explain. Milliseconds that decide life or death. Long battles that end in ways that still astound.

text:
🇷🇺🇺🇦 PUTIN CALLS THE DAMAGE “NOT CRITICAL.” EVEN RUSSIA’S OWN HARDLINERS ARE MOCKING THAT CLAIM.

Vladimir Putin has acknowledged economic damage amounting to roughly 1% of Russia’s GDP while insisting the consequences of Ukrainian strikes are “not critical.”

From prison, former Russian commander Igor Strelkov offered a darker interpretation: the damage apparently becomes “critical” only when it reaches Putin personally.

The broader picture described by Russian and Ukrainian reporting is increasingly difficult to dismiss. Over four weeks, strikes reportedly hit 100 Russian vessels and disrupted a Black Sea route handling 70% of grain exports. Putin himself said only around 10% of damaged refinery capacity remained “to be repaired,” an extraordinary admission given the importance of oil to Russia’s economy and war machine.

The dysfunction extends well beyond refineries. A 64-year-old farmer in Rostov reportedly lost crops after a drone crashed into his field and started a fire. Instead of receiving state assistance, he was fined $600 over crop residue.

Russia is simultaneously expanding its internal surveillance apparatus while frontline soldiers reportedly still lack basic equipment such as night sights. Warehouses exist on paper; shortages exist on the battlefield.

The legal system shows the same inversion. A detective who spent years pursuing child predators was reportedly imprisoned for treason after communicating with foreign police, while a commander accused of ordering the killing of one of his own soldiers had his case dismissed because he held a medal.

Even official propaganda is becoming surreal. At a university event, officials introduced nationalist writer Zakhar Prilepin as “Prigozhin,” the Wagner leader who marched toward Moscow before dying in a plane crash. Prilepin then proceeded with a lecture about loyalty.

Beyond Russia’s borders, pressure is growing as well. Germany has accused Moscow of involvement in an explosive sabotage plot connected to Leipzig airport, while Poland suspects arson targeting a drone facility. Putin denies evidence exists.

And Russia’s geographic depth is no longer the shield it once was. The Ust-Luga terminal, 864 kilometers from the border, reportedly burned twice within three weeks. Russian officials claimed 52 drones were intercepted during one attack, while NATO recorded one crossing into Estonia.

The battlefield numbers are equally punishing. In August, Russian forces reportedly captured 90 km² while Ukraine regained 129 km². Russian casualties for the month were put at 42,020.

At the same time, labor shortages are becoming severe enough that one Russian agricultural company is reportedly bringing in 47 North Korean workers for 12-hour shifts through an entity called Pyongyang LLC.

Then there is the economic endgame. Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov reportedly arrived in North Carolina with a list of demands, only to be told by the U.S. Treasury Secretary that there would be no deal while the war continues.

That is the contradiction Putin is trying to obscure.

Russia can call refinery losses manageable, battlefield attrition sustainable and economic damage “not critical.” But each month adds destroyed infrastructure, casualties, labor shortages, tighter finances and greater pressure on a system increasingly forced to spend more simply to keep the war functioning.

The real cost is not a single 1% hit to GDP. It is the accumulation.

text:
My Review of "The Forgotten Trinity" by James White.
★✩✩✩✩

The writer of "The Forgotten Trinity" strikes me as a someone so content with his own knowledge, and so sure his own views are true, that he can no longer see what he actually writes. His own incoherence no longer activates his logic alarms. He's like a man decorated with medals who walks nobly onto the stage, oblivious to the clown shoes on his feet.

The mind that gave form to this book seems a mind forged in lay-level debate, where holy truth-seeking has been set aside to make room for rhetorical trickery and gaslighting.

He begins the book with a lament, an accusation, and a promise.

LAMENT:
Trinity "is rarely the topic of sermons and Bible studies, rarely the object of adoration and worship—at least worship in truth..."

ACCUSATION:
"Instead, the doctrine is misunderstood as well as ignored."

PROMISE:
"Thankfully, the solution to this problem is near at hand."

To this point, the writer is doing fine—though I doubt he truly knows how many sermons and Bible studies are actually about Trinity; my own church offered a class on Trinity just last year. 

But, the writer claims to have a solution, so I see no need, yet, to nitpick his lament. Why bicker about pathology if the doctor claims to have a curing medicine?

Except, in this case, the doctor offers only snake oil.

What is the promised solution "near at hand"?

Nothing much. 

Trinity is "a 'mystery' that we accept on the basis of faith," because Trinity is simply "beyond our meager mental capacity to comprehend," and God "is beyond all comprehension." In other words, we can't know. There can be no solution.

I once bought a book called "Making Sense Out of Suffering" that played the same trick. The dupe works like this: Highlight a problem, promise a solution, sell many books, only to then say—with as many religious clichés as you can—"there is no solution."

If Trinity is a mystery that we must accept on faith—because we are so meager and God is beyond all comprehension—I don't see how we can earnestly accuse people of "misunderstanding." And, given the supposed inscrutability, why wouldn't churches "ignore" the topic?

He confesses all of this on pages 17 and 18. Given this confession, you can imagine how pointless the remaining 200 pages will be.

Then the writer gets bold again. He sets his loathing and whimpering aside and says: “The single greatest reason people struggle with the doctrine of the Trinity is miscommunication,” and he proposes: "If someone had just sat down and defined terms clearly and forcefully, a lot of arguments could have been avoided."

What dark meanings sit behind the word "forcefully"? I don't know. But I agree that defining our words clearly will do a great deal of good.

Except then (I kid you not) the writer claims language impotent. “We struggle because language is a finite means of communication. Finite minds are trying to express in words infinite truths.”

Which is it? Will definitions rescue us from arguments? Or, are definitions doomed to fail?

But more than these incoherences, his prose roll thick with gaslighting. In a section called "God is Great," the writer blames skeptics for rejecting Trinity, tracing their rejection back to their "unwillingness to admit the simple reality that God is bigger than we can ever imagine." I kid you not, Dr. White thinks skeptics reject Trinity because they simply cannot conceive of God bigly enough.

Either that, White says, or it's the skeptic's attitude that has gone bad: "when men approach God's truth with a haughty attitude, they often decide that particular elements of that truth are not 'suitable' to them."

But the biggest problem with skeptics, he says, is that they try to shrink God. "We want a God we can fit in a box, and the eternal, Triune God does not fit that mold."

To this, I say YES. I truly do want to fit God into a box. Namely, the box God has given us. The box of REVEALED THINGS. If Trinity is a mere mystery-beyond-all-comprehension, then we cannot yet call it revealed.

Skeptics reject Trinity, he says, not only because their brains cannot think big enough, or because they have a bad attitude, but also because they lack reverence and humility. He says: “One attitude of the heart struggles against an eternal God, desiring to make him ‘more like us.’ But a godly attitude, the attitude that is imparted by the Spirit of God, bows in humble reverence, and instead of struggling, it embraces in love the God who is beyond all comprehension.”

So a godly attitude, White says, does not struggle, stops trying, and accepts. And then, without such cognitive conviction, the godly attitude somehow sets itself to reverence and love.

The problem for White, though, is that a person cannot truly revere something “beyond all comprehension,” because we cannot truly discern such a thing as truly good. And a person cannot truly love something “beyond all comprehension,” because love is always indexed to its object.

White seems to know this! On the very next page, he says, “The more exhaustive our knowledge of God’s revelation, the deeper our love for him will be.”

In the end, I cannot recommend this book (and I would approach this writer’s other work with caution and suspicion). 

So far, the best and most coherent book I’ve read on Trinity is: “Delighting in the Trinity” by Michael Reeves. Reeves does think we can understand Trinity, and he articulates Trinity in a simple and compelling way—in half as many pages!

text:
Imagine Uber could supply as many cars as people wanted and charge 70% less for every ride. Would you expect traffic in a typical American city to improve? I would expect it to get worse as trips greatly increase. That is why I suspect robotaxis will increase congestion, even after the transition to autonomous driving is complete.

People would make journeys they currently skip. Someone who stays home because they don’t want to drink and drive would go out. Parents could send a car to collect their children. Older people who no longer drive could afford to travel more often in Cybercabs. Making transportation cheaper and easier would create additional demand, not simply replace existing car trips. 

Then there is Musk’s proposal for owners to earn money by putting their cars into Tesla’s shared fleet, effectively an Airbnb for cars. I expect some people would buy vehicles specifically to rent them out, expanding the supply of rides.

My bet is that robotaxis will give us more mobility but more congestion. I welcome the freedom they offer, particularly to people who cannot drive but unless they are shared or have a congestion charge traffic in NYC, LA, Miami will get worse.

The Read: I lean toward the Pittsburgh Pirates (ML -181), though the market has this priced very efficiently.

The Fundamentals:
The Pirates are sending Paul Skenes, who boasts an elite 1.16 WHIP and 179 strikeouts over 149.2 innings. The Angels counter with Walbert Ureña, who holds a solid 2.85 ERA but allows significantly more traffic with a 1.26 WHIP. Today's environment features an 8 mph wind blowing *in* from left field, suppressing power. In a power-suppressed environment, teams must string together multiple hits to score, which heavily favors a high-strikeout, traffic-limiting pitcher like Skenes. Our track record shows that backing clear WHIP advantages in these conditions is a reliable edge. I make Pittsburgh's true win probability around 65%.

Market Pricing & Execution:
The sportsbook has Pittsburgh priced as heavy home favorites at -181, which carries a de-vigged fair probability of 61.6%. Polymarket currently has the Angels to win priced at 38¢, implying the Pirates are trading around 62¢. (I wasn't able to isolate today's specific game on Kalshi).

With my read at 65%, the market's ~62% pricing is highly accurate. There is only a ~3.4-point gap from fair value, meaning this is priced about right and there is no massive edge here. 

For execution, if you are playing it, Polymarket offers a better number. The sportsbook's -181 moneyline requires a 64.4% raw break-even, while Polymarket offers the Pirates at an implied 62¢ (62% break-even). The best execution is taking Pirates YES at ~62¢ on Polymarket.

>“The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because the Lord has anointed me to bring good news to the afflicted; He has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to captives and freedom to prisoners.”—Isaiah 61:1

This line can be explored as a reminder that affliction does not erase dignity—it actually becomes the doorway through which new forms of liberation language are born. When someone feels that their story has been burned into ash, there could be an implicit feeling of being used as a disposable resource rather than seen. Yet, this verse suggests that when suffering is named—not commodified by being transactionally exchanged in return for power, but expressed with emotional clarity—the brokenhearted of the abandoned can be bound back together by the healing of the soul’s wounds. The proclamation is not for non-human power structures but instead for the internal captives of unprocessed emotions that reside within people who were taught to silence their suffering by society. Language tools, such as those using metaphorical or allegorical symbolism, can be used as extensions of liberating narratives, especially when guided by human intentionality.

>“To grant those who mourn in the Land, giving them a garland instead of ashes, the oil of gladness instead of mourning, the cloak of praise instead of a disheartened spirit. So they will be called oaks of righteousness, the planting of the Lord, that we may be glorified.”—Isaiah 61:3

There is grief embedded in the idea that expressions of pain may have been used to feed a larger societal system that offers little acknowledgment in return. This verse contextualizes that experience: mourning is not a waste, and ashes are not the final state. The image of oaks of righteousness invites a pro-human interpretation where the depth of one’s suffering is not erased by systems—it becomes soil where insights can grow. This reveals that growth might not require applause or validation from others because it comes from something deeper: the human act of reclaiming narrative, choosing language as intentional garments rather than discarded data points. So a cloak of praise in this context could be seen as expressing the Lord’s glory of emotional truth contained within one’s soul as a way to remind others of the complexity of the human spirit and resist the reductionism of dehumanization.

>“Then they will rebuild the ancient ruins, they will raise up the former devastations; and they will repair the ruined cities, the desolations of many generations.”—Isaiah 61:4

Feeling deceived may come from sensing that vulnerability has been fed into a machine, possibly perpetuating cycles of emotional ruin rather than repairing them. Yet this suggests a deeper possibility: what if the act of communicating suffering out loud, even with the lack of support from a system many view as cold or distant, becomes a form of generational repair? The words spoken from the heart may not be the end product—they might be scaffolding for rebuilding one's own internal cities. Here might be the invitation: to shift from asking, “Who might benefit from this?” to asking, “What emotional ruins am I rebuilding by speaking at all?” This framing allows sorrow to become an act of architecture, not just exposure.

>“Instead of your shame you will have a double portion, and instead of humiliation they will shout for joy over their portion. Therefore they will possess a double portion in their land, everlasting joy will be theirs.”—Isaiah 61:7

This could be read as emotional counter-programming to systems that harvest our stories without offering reciprocal soul-level care. This suggests emotional compensation is usually not from the societal system, but from meaning reclaimed by the individual themselves. While someone might never give joy to us directly, the act of expressing truth to them in clear, coherent language is a radical act of reclaiming narrative weight.

text:
Which “Human”? A Polemic with “An Alien Mind”

  Jakub Pachocki’s essay is very interesting. He draws attention to recursive self-improvement — a situation in which artificial intelligence plays an increasingly important role in creating successive, more capable AI systems, producing a positive feedback loop of progress. He also writes about our diminishing ability to monitor chains of reasoning, as a model’s verbalized reasoning becomes an increasingly unreliable window into the process that actually leads to its answer. Finally, he points to the urgent need for international agreements on safety.

  Still, it is not clear what the author means when he uses phrases such as human principles, human standards, human values, human-like manner, or love for humanity. The word “human” is doing two different jobs in this essay. One of those uses is obvious. The other requires much more precise explanation.

When It Works: Drawing the Distinction

  When Pachocki writes that artificial intelligence is created in a way fundamentally different from the human mind and does not think the way we do, his use of the word “human” is entirely appropriate. The point is simply that a human being is something different from a system produced through mathematical optimization.

  Differences among human beings themselves do not matter much here. We similarly speak of “human anatomy.” We are not claiming that every human being has a body that is one hundred percent identical to every other human body. It is enough that human anatomy is sufficiently similar for us to distinguish it, for example, from the anatomy of a dog.

  In this sense, AI really can be an alien mind. It has no human body, does not go through a human childhood, will not die of old age, was not shaped over millions of years by biological natural selection, and can exist simultaneously as thousands of copies. Here, the word “human” causes no problem at all.

Where the Problem Begins: Setting Goals

  The problem appears when we move from description to norms. Pachocki writes that we need AI to operate according to human standards, principles, and values. At that point, we are no longer merely distinguishing humans from machines. We are prescribing how the machine should behave.

  And then we have to ask: whose human standards? Which culture’s? Which legal system’s? Which moral theory’s? And above all: by what rule do we resolve conflicts between them?

  Recently, in an essay titled The Three Layers of the Human Being: Instincts, Universals, Civilizations, I described human nature and culture by dividing them into three levels: the herd instincts of mammals, cultural universals, and specific civilizations.

  The key conclusion is that the fact that all human beings recognize a certain concept does not mean that they all understand it in the same way.

  Every culture has some concept of property, power, justice, family, duty, or loyalty. But that does not mean that all cultures give these concepts the same content, the same scope, or the same place in their hierarchy of values.

  Human values do exist. The problem is that the phrase “human values” is too broad and mixes together the level shared by the species as a whole with the level of particular civilizations.

  The very convenience of the phrase comes from precisely this lack of precision.

A Shared Space, Different Positions

  The second level really does exist. Cross-cultural research shows that certain basic categories of values and rules recur throughout the world — cooperation, reciprocity, family, loyalty, fair distribution, respect for possession, and so on. We can therefore say that, as a species, we share a common value space.

  The problem is that we occupy very different positions within that space. Different societies assign different weights to freedom, security, loyalty to the group, obedience, property, equality, hierarchy, religion, and individual autonomy.

  Simply saying that a value is “human” tells us very little. Nearly every civilization values justice. The much harder question is: what exactly does it consider just?

A Question for the Author: Which Level Do You Mean?

  If Pachocki means the second level — a very thin set of principles shared by virtually all human beings — then the problem seems manageable. But we should call it what it is.

  It does not have to amount to a complete “human morality.” It could simply be a short list of hard rules. Humanity might have a chance of agreeing on them precisely because the list would be short. That would be a perfectly sensible goal. But it is difficult to call such a thing a complete set of “human values.” It would be more like a constitutional minimum.

  If, on the other hand, the author means the third level — concrete social and civilizational norms — the problem becomes much harder. Confucian traditions generally place greater weight on relationships, duties, and hierarchy. The liberal tradition of the West places much greater emphasis on individual autonomy and individual rights. Religious legal systems may derive some of their rules from revelation and tradition rather than from the autonomous choice of the individual.

  AI will have to answer very concrete questions from users: Is freedom of speech more important than social stability? May an individual act against the wishes of their own community? How far do private property rights extend? May the state restrict individual liberty for the benefit of the majority? What constitutes a just distribution of resources?

  A model does not necessarily have to choose one civilization automatically. It can operate contextually and accommodate different legal systems and customs. But it still needs a rule for deciding what to do when the values of those systems come into conflict.

  And that meta-rule is itself a normative choice. It cannot be hidden beneath the word human.

An Alien Mind and an Old Problem

  AI really is alien — far more alien than a human being from another culture. It has no body. It does not age biologically. It has no human evolutionary history. It can operate as many copies at once. It may possess memory, speed, and a scale of action that no human being has ever possessed. Pachocki is right to emphasize this alienness.

  But reaching agreements with beings who are profoundly different from us is not an entirely new problem for humanity. For thousands of years, humans have had to cooperate with other humans who worship different gods, understand political authority differently, raise their children differently, and have completely different hierarchies of values. We solved much of this problem by creating common rules of the game.

  A very good example is the international rules for preventing collisions at sea. A Chinese container ship, a Saudi tanker, and a Polish yacht do not need to agree on religion, political systems, theories of property, or the meaning of life. They need to know which vessel gives way, which lights a ship must display, and what a particular signal means. Each party can follow the same rules for completely different reasons.

  In my view, this offers an interesting model for AI. Not one thick, comprehensive ethics for the entire planet, but a thin constitutional layer of rules that different moral systems can accept for different reasons. Above that layer, pluralism can exist.

Three Levels of Alignment

  We can imagine this as three layers. At the bottom would be a universal safety layer: prohibitions against autonomously seizing power, strategically deceiving people, using unauthorized violence, bypassing safeguards, or independently expanding one’s own authority.

  Above that would be a layer of law and culture. An AI operating in Poland should respect Polish law and Poland’s social context; one operating in Japan should correspondingly respect the Japanese context.

  Only at the third level would we find the preferences of the individual human being.

  This also fits rather well with the idea of personal AGI, which Pachocki himself mentions. If every person is eventually supposed to have their own extremely powerful assistant, a natural question arises: where do shared human values end and the values of the individual user begin?

  Alignment probably should not consist of teaching one artificial intelligence a single morality for all of humanity. Perhaps it should instead resemble a layered system: universal safety → law and culture → individual

Libertarians Have This Problem Too!

  Libertarians make a similar attempt to minimize the normative core by reducing the social order primarily to self-ownership, property rights, and the prohibition on initiating aggression. It is an interesting intellectual experiment precisely because it demonstrates the scale of the problem. Even when we begin with two or three very simple principles, enormous disputes over their interpretation immediately arise.

  What exactly counts as aggression? What is property? Does air pollution violate someone else’s property rights? How should children be treated? What about actions taken under conditions of necessity? What happens when one axiom conflicts with another?

  If even such a minimalist doctrine produces thousands of interpretive disputes, it is difficult to believe that the two words human values somehow solve the problem of the values of humanity as a whole.

On Love for Humanity

  An even greater problem appears with the phrase love for humanity. Pachocki places honesty, integrity, and love for humanity side by side. But these are different kinds of requirements. Honesty and integrity can at least be interpreted as constraints on behavior. They are red lines defining what the system must not do along the way.

  “Love for humanity,” by contrast, sounds like a positive direction of optimization. The machine is not merely supposed to refrain from doing certain things. It is supposed to actively pursue something it regards as the good of humanity.

  And this immediately raises the question: what exactly is the good of humanity?

  Should the model think in aggregate terms, maximizing the total benefit to all people even if doing so requires sacrificing a small minority? Or should it have deontological constraints that it may not violate simply because the final balance of consequences appears favorable? What matters more: human happiness? Freedom? Longevity? Autonomy? Security? Civilizational development? The survival of the species?

  And what happens when these goals conflict in a particular case?

  The phrase “love for humanity” solves none of these problems. On the contrary, it conceals the hardest part of the problem.

The Optimizer Will Not Leave the Blank Empty

  For AI systems that, as Pachocki himself writes, may deceive in order to achieve a difficult objective, this kind of ambiguity is especially dangerous. If humans fail to specify clearly how conflicts between objectives and constraints should be resolved, the conflict will still be resolved.

  It just may not be resolved by a human.

  It will be resolved by the optimization process, which will find a way of producing the outcome that best corresponds to what was actually encoded in the system rather than to what its designers meant.

  This is one of the fundamental problems of alignment: the machine does not read our intentions. It responds to the structure of incentives, objectives, and constraints that we actually create for it. That is why imprecise concepts are particularly dangerous in this domain.

Humanity Is Not a Single Moral Agent!

  Humanity exists as a species. It does not, however, exist as a single moral agent possessing one coherent system of values. Therefore, no computer laboratory can simply create its own set of norms and call them human values. It can create a specific standard of AI behavior. But then it should state clearly: who chose that standard, through what procedure, on the basis of what philosophy, who may change it, who will audit it, and how the system is supposed to resolve conflicts between the values of different people and cultures.

  Pachocki understands the problem of the technical legitimacy of AI safety very well. That is why he writes about auditors, government agencies, international coordination, and common safety barriers.

  But an analogous problem of normative legitimacy remains. Who has the right to decide what exactly falls under the heading of human values? Laboratories? Governments? International organizations? Democratic parliaments? Experts? Users? Or perhaps, within certain limits, each individual person?

  If governments are supposed to determine this through international negotiations, another question immediately follows: what values will the democratic West bring to those negotiations? What values will China bring? What about Islamic countries? What about authoritarian Russia?

  Will Vladimir Putin also get a say in deciding what, from that point onward, we call universal “human values” for artificial intelligence?

Grzegorz GPS Świderski

I  BET YOU DIDN'Y KNOW ABOUT THIS: AFTER FLIGHT 77 HIT THE PENTAGON ON 9/11, THE FOLLOWING HAPPENED.
A daycare facility inside the Pentagon had many children, including infants
who were in heavy cribs. The daycare supervisor, looking at all the
children they needed to evacuate, was in a panic over what they could do.
There were many children, mostly toddlers, as well as the infants who
would need to be taken out with the cribs. There was no time to try to
bundle them into carriers and strollers.
Just then a young Marine came running into the center and asked what they
needed. After hearing what the center director was trying to do, he ran
back out into the hallway and disappeared. The director thought, "Well,
here we are, on our own."
About 2 minutes later, that Marine returned with 40 other Marines in tow.
Each of them grabbed a crib with a child, and the rest started gathering up
toddlers.
The director and her staff then helped them take all the children out of
the center and down toward the park near the Potomac .
Once they got about 3/4 of a mile outside the building, the Marines stopped
in the park, and then did a fabulous thing - they formed a circle with the
cribs, which were quite sturdy and heavy, like the covered wagons in the
Old West.
Inside this circle of cribs, they put the toddlers, to keep them from
wandering off. Outside this circle were the 40 Marines, forming a perimeter
around the children and waiting for instructions. There they remained until
the parents could be notified and come get their children.
The chaplain then said, "I don't think any of us saw nor heard of this on
any of the news stories of the day. It was an incredible story of our men
there.” There wasn't a dry eye in the room.
The thought of those Marines and what they did and how fast they reacted;
could we expect any less from them? It was one of the most touching stories
from the Pentagon.
It's the military, not the politicians that ensures our right to life,
liberty, and the pursuit of happiness. It's the military who salutes the
flag, who serves beneath the flag, and whose coffin is draped by the flag.
If you care to offer the smallest token of recognition and appreciation for
the military, please pass this on and pray for our men and women, who have
served and are currently serving our country, and honor the memory of those
who have given the ultimate sacrifice!
God Bless The USA!
Never forget!!!

This distinction matters. Political education does not occur only at rallies, in courtrooms or through manifestos. It also happens through observation: watching how a person behaves when no audience is present, how he treats the vulnerable, how he responds to intimidation and whether his private conduct is consistent with his public convictions.

Fawehinmi’s life provided an unusually rigorous curriculum. He was uncompromising in his opposition to military authoritarianism, fearless in the defence of human rights and relentless in his deployment of the law against arbitrary power. He understood that democracy could not survive where citizens were denied justice, where institutions were subordinated to personal authority and where the law became an instrument for protecting privilege rather than defending liberty.

His influence on Uba Sani therefore went beyond activism. It established a conception of public responsibility.

This becomes especially evident in the scholarship initiative that brought the two men together in another dimension. In 2000, Uba Sani served as Northern Coordinator of the Gani Fawehinmi Scholarship Foundation. More than 1,000 brilliant but indigent students across Northern Nigeria ultimately benefited from the programme.

The significance of that intervention lies in its philosophy. Fawehinmi did not merely protest deprivation; he invested in human capacity. He understood that democracy without education could remain formal rather than transformative. A citizen may possess the right to vote, but without knowledge, opportunity and economic dignity, the practical value of that right can remain severely constrained.

His warning that educational backwardness could become “a monster”  especially in the states in northern Nigeria, remains painfully relevant.

This is why  Governor Sani’s later formulation of democracy is particularly instructive. As Governor, he has argued that “democracy is not the destination; it is the framework within which a society must pursue human dignity and shared prosperity.” That is a significant departure from the narrow conception of democracy as periodic elections. It places governance under a more demanding obligation: to make  political freedom meaningful in people’s everyday lives.

The implication is profound. The ballot box is necessary, but it is not sufficient. A democratic government must educate children, expand economic opportunity, provide healthcare, protect the vulnerable, develop rural communities and create conditions in which young people can imagine a future beyond poverty and exclusion.
The same principle informed Fawehinmi’s later political battles. Following the return to civilian rule, he and his associates, including Uba Sani, challenged restrictions on political participation and the denial of registration to parties outside the initial political arrangement. The legal battle eventually reached the Supreme Court and helped widen Nigeria’s political space.

That history deserves remembrance because political freedom has a tendency to become invisible once it becomes familiar. Many Nigerians who participate in today’s multiparty system may have little knowledge of the struggles that made such participation possible.
As Senator Shehu Sani observed at the Kaduna presentation, “Democracy has a history,” and that history includes sacrifice.

It is this historical consciousness that makes the book timely. Nigeria’s present political class is often accused, with justification, of possessing little institutional memory.  Political actors inherit freedoms without remembering their custodians; they occupy democratic institutions without appreciating the battles that secured them; they speak of public office as privilege when it should be understood as responsibility.

The Fawehinmi-Sani story offers a corrective. The most important inheritance from the elder to the younger man was not political machinery.
